title-group.article-title: Nature-Based Solutions: Examining the Effects of Small Artificial Ponds on Insect Diversity and Their Implications for the Brazilian Semi-Arid Region

abstract.p: Small artificial ponds, known as barraginhas, play a crucial role in providing essential ecosystem services such as soil and water conservation in semi-arid regions. Despite their effectiveness and widespread use in the Brazilian semi-arid region, their effects on biodiversity remain unexplored. Here, we conducted a field experiment to evaluate whether barraginhas constructed along roads to prevent soil erosion influence the diversity of terrestrial insects, specifically ants and beetles. A total of four sampling events were conducted at the beginning and end of both the dry and rainy seasons to assess the effects of the interaction between barraginhas and intra- and interseasonal variation on beetle and ant assemblages. Overall, ant species richness was higher at the end of the rainy season, whereas beetle species richness peaked at the beginning of the rainy season, followed by a secondary peak at the end of rainy season. Importantly, our results showed that barraginhas did not affect beetle richness, whereas ant species richness was significantly higher in barraginha treatment at the end of the rainy season. This seasonal pattern should be interpreted cautiously, as no consistent effect of barraginhas on ant species richness was detected across sampling periods. Ant species composition varied across all sampling months but was not influenced by barraginhas. Similarly, beetle species composition was unaffected by barraginhas and did not differ among the analyzed sampling moths. Given the ecological and economic importance of insects and their global decline across many taxa and functional groups, initiatives to promote conservation and enhance local biodiversity are critical. Finally, we suggest conducting similar studies in different environments and across various taxonomic groups, including plants, other invertebrates, and vertebrates, since barraginhas can also contribute to biodiversity enhancement specially in arid and semi-arid regions.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Semi-arid regions with unpredictable weather, long dry seasons, inconsistent rainfall, and soils poor in nutrients cover approximately 15% of the Earth’s land surface and support 14.4% of the global population [1,2]. The semi-arid tropics include parts of 48 developing countries including India, locations in Southeast Asia, a swathe across sub-Saharan Africa, Southern and Eastern Africa, and disjunct areas of Latin America [2,3,4,5]. In Brazil, according to resolution number 150/2021 CONDEL/SUDENE (Deliberative Council of the Northeast Development Superintendence), the semi-arid region occupies an area of approximately 1.6 million km2 distributed among 11 states of the Federation (see also Figure 1). It is home to around 53.1 million inhabitants, representing the world’s most populous semi-arid region [6]. This region is distinguished as a drought hotspot due to persistent large-scale disruptions in the tropospheric circulation patterns [7], as well as deforestation and agricultural expansion that increase climate severity, soil degradation and biodiversity loss [8].

The Brazilian semi-arid region harbors four different biomes: Caatinga, Cerrado, Amazon, and Atlantic Forest. The climate pattern varies from the dry inland to the humid Atlantic coast, with rainfall increasing steadily from the semi-arid interior toward the coast [9]. Generally, the climate is marked by seasonality, with the wettest season typically occurring from December to April, while the dry season extends from May to October [10]. The Caatinga and Cerrado are dominant in Brazilian semi-arid regions, covering approximately 71.5% and 20.6% of the region, respectively [2] (Figure 1). The Caatinga, a restricted biome of Brazil, has vegetation that varies from deciduous low shrubs to small patches of tall dry forests. Rainfall in the Caatinga has extremely irregular temporal and geographical distributions [11]. The Cerrado vegetation (Brazilian savanna) varies from closed- to open-canopy deciduous and semi-deciduous vegetation with a maximum height of 15 m, to shrubs and natural grasslands [12].

Despite its high species diversity, extreme levels of endemism, and the essential ecosystem services provided by the Brazilian semi-arid ecosystem, this natural environment has been extensively converted, particularly into agricultural land, silviculture with exotic species, and pasture [2,13]. For instance, estimates show a 37.16% loss in forest cover in the Brazilian semi-arid between 2000 and 2018 [2,4]. Maintaining native vegetation cover is crucial for preserving moisture, ensuring soil formation, preventing erosion, and ultimately ecosystem functioning, particularly in semi-arid environments where rainfall is concentrated in short periods each year [4]. Ecological restoration of deforested areas in the semi-arid region is also a highly complex task due to the unique characteristics of the soil, the severity of the climate, and the high species diversity and endemism [13]. Furthermore, climate projections indicate an increase in the frequency, duration, and severity of droughts in the Brazilian semi-arid region [14], leading to land degradation and desertification [15,16]. It is therefore urgent to develop a comprehensive understanding of techniques for the sustainable management of natural resources and the restoration of degraded areas. This knowledge is essential for ensuring both ecosystem preservation and the social development of this vast region.

Various edaphic, vegetation, and mechanical techniques have been employed to attempt mitigate the effects of prolonged droughts, preserve and restore degraded soils, aid in water retention, and recharge underground aquifers in semi-arid regions [3,17]. Among these, the EMBRAPA (Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa Agropecuária) has developed the “Barraginhas Project” which focuses on constructing small ponds strategically placed along runoff paths in fields, pastures, and road edges. These small ponds (hereafter referred to as barraginhas) reduce the speed of surface runoff, mitigating erosion processes that could lead to the formation of gullies and siltation of water bodies [18]. Additionally, these barraginhas act as retention basins, collecting rainwater, thereby increasing local moisture and recharging groundwater reservoirs [19]. Despite their effectiveness and widespread use for soil and water preservation, particularly in the Brazilian semi-arid region, the impact of barraginhas on local biodiversity has yet to be thoroughly assessed.

Humidity is a climatic factor that influences the fitness, reproductive behavior and geographic distribution of animals and plants worldwide [20,21,22]. Insects are crucial components of biodiversity [23,24,25], contributing significantly to ecosystem functioning and providing numerous ecosystem services [26,27,28]. Given their generally small body size, and the fact that most insect species are ectothermic, these organisms are especially susceptible to changes in environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity [21,29]. Various natural factors, such as climatic seasonality, the presence of water bodies, and the type of soil vegetation cover, affect humidity and, consequently, the local insect fauna [30,31,32]. For example, in semi-arid regions, generally insect species diversity tends to increase during the early rainy season [33,34,35], but this pattern can be influenced by intra-seasonal climatic variations and guild-specific traits [34,36]. Additionally, abiotic changes associated with human activities, such as irrigation and the construction of water reservoirs, can also enhance humidity levels and increase local arthropod diversity [21,32].

Ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) and beetles (Coleoptera) are two highly diverse insect groups that respond quickly to microenvironmental changes at small scales [37,38,39]. These characteristics, along with their relatively well-known taxonomy, enable researchers to characterize the relationship between changes in the community structure of these two insect groups and human-induced environmental alterations in their habitats [36,40,41]. In this study, we conducted a field experiment during both the dry and wet seasons to investigate whether barraginhas constructed along roads to prevent soil erosion could influence the community structure of ants and beetles in a transitional Caatinga/Cerrado area in the Brazilian semi-arid region. Specifically, we expected that: (i) the presence of barraginhas will increase the local diversity of ants and beetles, as these structures accumulate rainwater and enhance environmental conditions for these animals; (ii) the positive influence of barraginhas on ant and beetle diversity will be stronger during the rainy season, given that these structures may lose their ecological functionality by desiccating during the extended dry season; and (iii) regardless of the presence of barraginhas, the diversity of these insect groups will increase during the rainy season, as they typically respond positively to seasonal increases in humidity.

sec.title: 2.1. Study Area
sec.p: Fieldwork was conducted in the Parque Estadual Caminho dos Gerais (PECG), located in the Serra Geral, southern portion of the Brazilian semi-arid region, at the extreme northern edge of Minas Gerais State, Brazil (Figure 1). The PECG covers approximately 56,000 hectares of plateaus, with an average elevation of 1090 m a.s.l., and features vegetation typical of the Caatinga and Cerrado Biomes. These biomes exhibit various vegetation types, including campos rupestres, seasonal dry forest, open Cerrado and Cerrado stricto sensu. The conservation unit was established in March 2007. Previously, much of the PECG area was used for the commercial cultivation of Eucalyptus species for charcoal production [42]. Areas that were used for Eucalyptus cultivation are still in the early stages of regeneration and are often intersected by abandoned roads experiencing varying intensities of soil erosion. The climate is semi-arid with well-defined dry and rainy seasons. The average annual temperature is 24 °C, and annual precipitation is about 830 mm, primarily concentrated between November and February [43] (see also Figure 2).

Specifically, fieldwork was conducted in a 40-hectare area of Cerrado that has undergone natural regeneration since the removal of a former Eucalyptus plantation in 2007, approximately 14 years before our sampling. The vegetation in this area consists of grasses, scattered shrubs and tree species, with no canopy connection, reaching heights of up to 3.5 m. The most common tree species in this area include Anadenanthera colubrina, Brosinum gaudichaudii, Copaifera arenicola, Dimorphandra molis, Eugenia dysenterica, Jacaranda decurrens, Plathymenia reticulata, Qualea spp. and Tachigali subvelutina [43]. This experimental area is intersected by two parallel abandoned roads, separated by 500 m. Originally, these roads were constructed to access Eucalyptus plantations and transport charcoal. However, with the establishment of the PECG, the roads were abandoned, and now exhibit gullies caused by surface runoff from rainwater. Between November and December 2021, eleven Barraginhas were constructed along the edges of one of these roads to mitigate soil erosion processes. These rectangular ponds, each measuring 5 m in length and 2 m in width, have a maximum depth of 2 m, and were spaced approximately 80 m apart.

sec.title: 2.2. Experimental Design
sec.p: A total of 60 pitfall traps were used to sample terrestrial insects, specifically ants and beetles, and assess the effects of barraginhas on their diversity. Each pitfall trap consisted of a 1 L plastic pot containing 500 mL of water and 5 mL of neutral detergent, buried level with the soil and left in the field for three consecutive days. During all sampling periods, pitfall traps were protected from rain and overflow by a cover suspended 5 cm above the rim of each trap using bamboo stakes, while still allowing insects to enter the traps. These 60 traps were evenly distributed between two transects, 500 m apart, along the two roads crossing in the experimental area. These two transects with 30 pitfall traps represent two different treatments (t1 = presence of barraginhas and t2 = absence of barraginhas). The pitfall traps were considered sampling units rather than independent experimental replicates, as each treatment was represented by a single transect. Therefore, the comparison between treatments is subject to pseudoreplication, and the results should be interpreted with caution. In each transect, the 30 traps were spaced approximately 30 m apart. In treatment t1, three pitfall traps were arranged linearly between two consecutive barraginhas (see Figure 3 for details). Four seasonal samplings were conducted: two during the rainy season (March 2022 and January 2023, corresponding to end and beginning of the rainy season, respectively) and two during the dry season (July 2022 and September 2022, corresponding to the beginning and end of the dry season, respectively). The insects collected were stored in containers with 70% ethyl alcohol and sent to the Center for Insect Biology and Taxonomy (INSECTA) at the State University of Montes Claros (Unimontes), where ants and beetles were sorted and identified on the basis of external morphology using taxonomic keys [44,45], identification guides [46], comparison with reference material deposited at INSECTA, and consultations with specialists.

sec.title: 2.3. Statistical Analyses
sec.p: Initially, we developed two different generalized linear models to test differences in ant and beetle richness among treatments and sampling periods as well as the interactions between these two variables. In these models, treatments, sampling period, and interactions were used as explanatory variables, while the richness of ants or beetles was used as the response variable. Respectively, for the models where ants or beetle richness was the response variable, the Poisson and Negative Binomial distributions were adopted. These models were tested using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) with the “Chisq” test. When the ANOVA results were significant (p < 0.05), contrast analyses were performed to group similar levels (p ≥ 0.05) and distinguish statistically different levels (p < 0.05). All analyses were conducted using the R software, version 4.4.0 [47].

To compare species composition of ants and beetles among treatments, sample period, and their interaction, we used a two-way permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) with 10,000 permutations, employing a Chord distance calculated from an abundance matrix. For beetles, only the collections made during the rainy season were included in this analysis, although 14 beetle species were recorded during the dry season (see Supplementary Material S2). Beetle activity was extremely low during this period. Of the 120 pitfall traps used to sample beetles, only 19 collected beetles, with just 7 and 12 traps containing beetles in July and September, respectively. Thus, most sampling units had zero captures during the dry season, resulting in an extremely sparse community matrix. Under these circumstances, we considered that including the dry-season samples in the PERMANOVA would provide limited and potentially unstable information about differences in community composition because the analysis would be strongly influenced by the predominance of zero values. When pairwise PERMANOVA indicated statistical differences (p < 0.05), we graphically illustrated data distributions using Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA). These analyses were performed using Past software (Paleontological Statistics, version 4.03, [48]).

sec.title: 3. Results
sec.p: The ant fauna sampled in the study area comprised 11,338 individuals distributed across seven subfamilies, 23 genera, and 33 species. The ant subfamily with the greatest species diversity was Myrmicinae (16 species), followed by Formicinae (six species) and Ectatomminae (four species) (Supplementary Material S1). The beetle fauna included 303 individuals belonging to 11 families, 26 genera, and 48 species. The most speciose Coleoptera families were Scarabaeidae and Curculionidae, with 15 and six species, respectively (Supplementary Material S2).

The ant species richness was not affected by the barraginha treatment, but varied in function of sampling periods and the interaction between those variables (Table 1). Contrast analyses revealed that ant richness was higher in March and did not vary across the other collection months. Additionally, the contrast analyses indicated that ant richness was positively affected by the barraginhas treatment only in March (Figure 4A, see also Supplementary Material S3). Beetle richness varied significantly only in function sampling months (Table 1). Contrast analyses revealed that beetle richness was highest in January, followed by March, with the lowest richness recorded in July and September (Figure 4B, see also Supplementary Material S3).

The ant species composition varied according to the sampling months but did not change based on treatments or the interaction between sampling months and treatments (Table 2). Pairwise PERMANOVA comparisons among months revealed that the ant species composition differed across all sampling months (Figure 5). In contrast, beetle species composition was not affected by barraginha treatments, sampling months, or the interaction between these variables during the rainy season. However, beetle species composition differed between rainy and dry seasons, with only 14 species recorded during the dry season compared with 40 species during the rainy season. This difference was accompanied by very low beetle activity during the dry season, with only 19 pitfall traps containing beetles, including 7 traps in July and 12 in September.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: Barraginhas built along road edges to control soil erosion also collect rainwater, thereby increasing local humidity and mitigating the effects of droughts in the Brazilian semi-arid region [18,49]. Insects generally respond positively to increased humidity, which can lead to higher population abundance and species diversity [21,30]. Given this context, we anticipated that barraginhas would enhance the diversity of ants and beetles. However, our results indicate that the construction of barraginhas had a limited impact on ant community structure and did not affect the beetle community. Specifically, the effect on the ant community was confined to a 26.2% increase in mean ant species richness, observed only in March, at the end of the rainy season. These findings suggest that while barraginhas may provide localized benefits in terms of increased ant diversity during specific periods, their effects on insect biodiversity may vary among taxonomic groups and sampling periods. Nevertheless, the relatively short interval between the construction of the barraginhas and the beginning of sampling should be considered when interpreting these results. The approximately three-month period may have provided limited time for insects to detect and colonize the newly created resource. Therefore, longer-term studies are needed to determine whether the effects of barraginhas on insect biodiversity become more evident over time.

The Brazilian semi-arid region not only experiences rainfall concentrated in a few months of the year, but also faces significant intra-seasonal variation, with drought periods occurring within the rainy season [9,19]. Barraginhas accumulate water during intermittent rainy periods, promoting therefore greater uniformity in soil moisture throughout the rainy season [17,18]. Ant colonization of new habitats typically involves the production of winged queens that leave the mother colony to establish new nests [40,50]. In the semi-arid regions, the production of winged queens and the subsequent founding of new ant colonies typically occur at the beginning of the rainy season [51]. Initially, the foraging activities of these new colonies are low and gradually increase over time [52]. Thus, the increase in average ant species richness in areas with the construction of barraginhas, observed only at the end of the rainy season, could be attributed to the local increase in soil moisture, which may attract winged queens early in the rainy season. The observed increase in ant species richness aligns with the period when new colonies intensify their foraging activities. These results suggest that barraginhas could positively influence ant colonization and community organization by stabilizing soil moisture, especially during critical reproductive periods. However, this hypothesis remains to be tested by future studies combining measurements of soil moisture with ant colony density and foraging activity across the rainy season. This has important implications for habitat management as enhancing local soil moisture through barraginhas can support ant biodiversity and contribute to more resilient ecosystems. Ants are involved in several ecosystem services [53] and effective implementation of nature-based solutions to habitat management could be a valuable strategy in habitat restoration and conservation efforts towards insect groups.

Our results also revealed significant intra- and inter-seasonal changes in the structure of ant and beetle communities. Overall, the average species richness of ants was higher at the end of the rainy season, while that of beetles was greater at the beginning of the season. It is also important to highlight the reduction in beetle species richness during the dry season, a pattern observed in other studies conducted in seasonal environments [36]. In the Brazilian semi-arid region, the onset of the rainy season is marked by an increased availability of resources, particularly due to the emission of new leaves by plants [35,36,54]. This period coincides with a rise in the abundance and activity of most insect species, which seek mating partners and more suitable sites for feeding and oviposition [55]. Therefore, the higher species richness of beetle observed at the beginning of the rainy season may be shaped by the synchronization of organisms’ life cycles with the availability of suitable resources in the environment. These findings underscore the critical role of seasonal dynamics in shaping insect community organizations and highlight the importance of maintaining habitat conditions that support these ecological processes. Effective habitat management strategies in semi-arid regions should consider the timing of resource availability and its impact on insect biodiversity to ensure the conservation of these vital fauna and the ecosystem services they provide.

Moreover, we observed that the total species richness of ants exhibited smaller intra- and inter-seasonal variation compared to the total species richness of beetles. Specifically, we recorded 29, 23, 24, and 26 ant species in March, July, September, and January, respectively. Additionally, the ant species composition varied across all sampling periods, suggesting the presence of a local pool of ant species that adapt their foraging activities in response to intra- and inter-seasonal climate changes [56]. Conversely, we sampled 17, 8, 9, and 34 beetle species in March, July, September, and January, respectively, indicating a significant decrease in beetle species richness during the dry season. The lack of difference in beetle species composition between the beginning and end of the wet season suggests strong intra-seasonal nesting within the beetle fauna, as evidenced by only five beetle species collected at the end of the rainy season that did not occur at the beginning. Overall, these findings highlight the varying responses of ants and beetles to seasonal changes, with ants showing more resilience to intra- and inter-seasonal fluctuations. This underscores the importance of considering species-specific responses and seasonal dynamics in habitat management and conservation strategies. By understanding these patterns, conservation efforts can be better tailored to maintain and enhance biodiversity to ensure stability and resilience in such semi-arid habitats.

The seasonal occurrence of insect species within the same habitat may be associated with behavioral variations in foraging and the organisms’ life cycle. For example, holo- or hemimetabolous species generally have low mobility during immature stages and are rarely captured by conventional traps used for sampling adult insects [30]. Thus, the low number of individuals of these species sampled during specific seasons may not necessarily indicate their absence from the habitat, but rather a sampling bias [34]. Conversely, short-term and non-seasonal changes in insect species richness within the same habitat likely involve events of local extinction or immigration. Several studies describe the loss of local insect diversity due to abrupt environmental changes, such as the conversion of natural areas into pastures [57], agricultural systems [58], homogeneous forests [59], and natural or anthropogenic disasters [60]. However, field experiments that manipulate abiotic factors such as humidity and temperature to create more favorable conditions for insects and promote the conservation or increase in local diversity remain quite rare. Initiatives of this kind should be prioritized, given the ecological and economic importance of insects, along with the current scenario of rapid declines in many insect populations across different taxa and functional groups worldwide (see [61] and the references therein).

Indeed, insects are important components of biodiversity and significantly contribute to ecosystem functioning through a series of services such as pollination, nutrient cycling, seed dispersal, and pest control [28,43,62]. Insects are particularly susceptible to changes in temperature and humidity, due to their small body mass and ectothermy [41,63]. In the current scenario of global climate change, coupled with the overuse of natural resources by humans in the Anthropocene, it is essential to move beyond traditional studies of species presence/absence in response to disturbances. This is necessary to protect and ensure the survival of insects and the essential services they provide. Developing new habitat management and restoration techniques will be vital for conserving insect species globally, especially in semi-arid regions that already face severe problems with desertification, soil overuse, and global warming. In this study, we found that barraginhas had limited effects on the diversity of two important insect groups (beetles and ants) in a regenerating Cerrado area in the Brazilian semi-arid region. Nevertheless, their well-documented benefits for soil conservation and the protection of water bodies provide important justification for their use as a complementary strategy for ecosystem conservation and restoration [3,17].

Finally, considering that this is the first study to investigate the relationship between barraginhas and local biodiversity in the Brazilian semi-arid region, as well as the potential for this soil and water conservation technique to serve as microclimatic refuges for biodiversity, we suggest some aspects that deserve attention in future studies: (i) characterizing the effects of barraginhas on different taxa, including plants, vertebrates, and other invertebrates, as well as on species interactions; (ii) assessing the effects of barraginha density (number per area) and spatial distribution (aligned, clustered, or random) on biodiversity; (iii) investigating the relationship between soil properties, especially the clay-to-sand ratio, and biodiversity, given their influence on water infiltration and local humidity; (iv) evaluating the influence of barraginhas on ecological succession over time; and (v) conducting studies with spatial replication, including multiple independent sampling sites with and without barraginhas, to disentangle the effects of barraginhas from potential differences among sites, such as soil properties, vegetation, and edge effects. This limitation should be considered when interpreting the results of the present study, as the sampling design did not allow us to fully separate the effects of barraginhas from those associated with differences among sites.

app.p: The following supporting information can be downloaded at: https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/conservation6040130/s1, Supplementary Material S1: Species/morphospecies richness and abundance of ants in relation to pond presence/absence and seasonal variation in Parque Estadual Caminhos dos Gerais, Minas Gerais, Brazil. Supplementary Material S2: Species/morphospecies richness and abundance of beetles in relation to pond presence/absence and seasonal variation in Parque Estadual Caminhos dos Gerais, Minas Gerais, Brazil. Supplementary Material S3: Rarefaction and extrapolation curves of ant (A) and beetle (B) species richness in relation to sampling abundance. Solid lines represent rarefaction, and dashed lines represent extrapolation. Shaded areas indicate 95% confidence intervals. Curves represent the four sampling periods (January, March, July, and September) under conditions with and without barraginhas. Different symbols indicate the observed species richness for each sampling period × treatment combination. The curves indicate (1) satisfactory sampling completeness, particularly for ants; (2) a positive effect of barraginhas on ant species richness in March, consistent with the GLM results reported in the main text; and (3) no clear differences in beetle species richness between treatments, but pronounced variation among sampling periods, reflecting seasonal differences between the rainy and dry seasons, as also described in the main text.
